Lewis Base-Catalyzed Interhalogenation of Terminal Allenes:
Selective Strategy for Accessing Vicinal Vinylic, Allylic
Heterodihalides
Alexandra E. Lubaev, Favour Eze, Manjula D. Rathnayake, and Liela Bayeh-Romero*
Cite This: Org. Lett. 2025, 27, 3527−3531

ABSTRACT: Though precedent remains limited, the selective interhalogenation of allenes ofers a valuable synthetic strategy to
access products where each halide exhibits orthogonal reactivity. Here, we describe a Lewis base-catalyzed approach for the
dihalogenation (bromochlorination, iodochlorination, iodobromination, and dibromination) of terminal allenes. By employing just 1
mol % of triphenylphosphine oxide or hexamethylphosphoramide to activate thionyl halides in the presence of electrophilic
halogenation reagents, we achieve the conversion of monosubstituted allenes to vicinal allylic, vinylic dihalides with up to 93% yield
and >20:1 regioisomeric ratio, favoring the branched dihalogenated product. A range of functional groups is tolerated, including
nitrile, ester, phosphate, sulfonamide, and silyl groups, and the reaction proved to be scalable. The utility of various dihalide products
was investigated in substitution and cross-coupling chemistry, highlighting the distinct reactivity among the diferent classes.

approaches for the incorporation of halogens into organic
frameworks is of increasing importance. Consequently, much
progress has been made over the past decade, including recent
work by our group, for the preparation of heterodihalides from
alkenes and alkynes (Figure 1a).<sup>5,6</sup>
By comparison, the interhalogenation of allenes is hardly
developed, despite recent advances in their selective function-
alization (Figure 1b).<sup>7</sup> Further, the utility of the resulting
heterodihalide products is apparent when one considers the
divergent reactivity profiles innate to allylic and vinylic halides
(e.g., nucleophilic displacement, cross coupling chemistry, etc.)
and the broad utility of alkenes as synthetic handles. For these
reasons, vicinal vinylic, allylic heterodihalides, though under-
explored, bear the capacity to serve as prized synthetic
lynchpins.
Strategies for allene interhalogenation are generally plagued
by issues of regio-, stereo-, and site-selectivity.<sup>7e,8</sup> The onerous
nature of these transformations is exemplified in the limited
number of reports detailing the bromochlorination of allenes
(Figure 1b). Two independent examples disclosed the use of
BrCl for the bromochlorination of propadiene or 2,3-
pentadiene.<sup>9</sup> However, these reactions sufer from low yields
and the presence of solvent-incorporated byproducts. In some
cases, solvolysis represented the major reaction pathway or no
yields were reported altogether, raising concerns as to the
overall eficiency of this transformation. During the course of
our studies, Katayev and co-workers disclosed a unique transfer
dihalogenation strategy applicable to allenes. However, only a
singular example of vicinal bromochlorination on an aryl-
substituted allene was demonstrated.<sup>10</sup>

dihalogenated product 2. To date, common methods
employed for allene dihalogenation are either unselective or
primarily feature linear product (3) selectivity with varying
levels of stereoselectivity.<sup>13,14</sup>

We commenced our investigations by surveying conditions
for allene bromochlorination. When 4,5-hexadienylbenzene
(1a) was subjected to thionyl chloride and a slight excess of N-
bromosuccinimide (NBS) in the absence of a catalyst, only
trace quantities of isomeric bromochlorides 2a and 3a were
observed (Table 1, entry 1). Instead, a significant amount of
undesired dibromination byproduct was observed. Under the
same conditions, but in the presence of 1 mol %
triphenylphosphine oxide, product was formed in 82% yield,
favoring branched bromochloride 2a with a 13:1 regioisomeric
ratio (rr) (entry 2).
While various solvents were generally suitable, trifluoroto-
luene proved optimal with respect to reaction eficiency and
selectivity (entries 2−4).<sup>15</sup> A survey of Lewis base catalysts
revealed triphenylphosphine oxide and hexamethylphosphor-
amide (HMPA) as superior catalysts, delivering up to 85%
yield (18:1 rr) at minimal loadings (entries 5−8). In the
examination of alternative bromenium sources, N-bromoph-
thalimide (NBP) provided optimal results, particularly when
used in combination with HMPA, afording bromochloride 2a
in 93% yield with 17.5:1 rr (entries 9−11). Further, the
reaction displays similar eficiency under noninert conditions
(entry 12).

examined the scope of this transformation (Table 2). In all

To investigate the utility of these uncommon vicinal vinylic,
allylic heterodihalides in organic synthesis, we chose to explore
the innate reactivity diferences between each class of dihalide
(Scheme 1).<sup>18</sup> Focusing initially on bromochlorides 2a and 2b,
we applied copper-catalyzed

allylic alkylation, yielding 4a
in 62% with an E/Z ratio >10:1.<sup>19</sup> In contrast,
S _ { \mathrm { N } } 2
displacement proved more challenging, though acetate 4b
was obtained in low yield.<sup>20</sup> To illustrate the utility of these
products for consecutive functionalization, enolate alkylation
to aford vinyl bromide 4c followed by Stille cross-coupling
gave an overall two-step yield of 53% of ester 4d.
Comparatively, the analogous iodochloride 2r demonstrated
poorer selectivity both in the copper-catalyzed allylic alkylation
(4e) and the direct substitution with KOAc (4f). A limitation
of the iodohalides, in general, is their bench instability,
necessitating rapid purification of the dihalide followed by
immediate setup for subsequent diversification reactions.
Nevertheless, iodobromide 2n exhibited superior
S _ { \mathrm { N } } 2 ^ { \prime }
reactivity with p-thiocresol (4g, 80% yield 1:5.7 E/Z) followed
by copper-catalyzed amide coupling of the vinyl iodide to
aford enamide 4h in 59% isolated yield.<sup>21,22</sup>
As anticipated, vicinal vinylic, allylic dibromides proved to
be the best compromise between the bromochlorides and the
iodohalides, owing to the lability of the allylic bromide
combined with the better stability of the vinyl bromide.
Probenecid-derived dibromide 2y could undergo highly
selective regiodivergent substitutions to aford vinyl bromides
4i and 4j in synthetically useful yields. Notably, palladium-
catalyzed Tsuji-Trost substitution with benzenesulfinate was
feasible without significant β-halo elimination to the allene, as
observed with other dihalide variants.<sup>23</sup>
In conclusion, we have developed a catalytic dihalogenation
of monosubstituted allenes, leading to vicinal vinylic and allylic
dihalides. Products were isolated in up to 93% yield and >20:1
regioselectivity using common electrophilic reagents in
combination with thionyl halides as latent nucleophiles
activated by simple Lewis base catalysts. This convenient
strategy for the synthesis of bromochlorides, iodochlorides,
iodobromides, and dibromides employs noncryogenic reaction
temperatures and low catalyst loadings of 1 mol %. The
resulting dihalides were evaluated as useful building blocks for
the preparation of a diverse range of functionalized di- and
trisubstituted alkenes.

To investigate the utility of these uncommon vicinal vinylic,
allylic heterodihalides in organic synthesis, we chose to explore
the innate reactivity diferences between each class of dihalide
(Scheme 1).<sup>18</sup> Focusing initially on bromochlorides 2a and 2b,
we applied copper-catalyzed
S _ { \mathrm { N } } \dot { 2 } ^ { \prime }
allylic alkylation, yielding 4a
in 62% with an E/Z ratio >10:1.<sup>19</sup> In contrast,
S _ { \mathrm { N } } 2
displacement proved more challenging, though acetate 4b
was obtained in low yield.<sup>20</sup> To illustrate the utility of these
products for consecutive functionalization, enolate alkylation
to aford vinyl bromide 4c followed by Stille cross-coupling
gave an overall two-step yield of 53% of ester 4d.
Comparatively, the analogous iodochloride 2r demonstrated
poorer selectivity both in the copper-catalyzed allylic alkylation
(4e) and the direct substitution with KOAc (4f). A limitation
of the iodohalides, in general, is their bench instability,
necessitating rapid purification of the dihalide followed by
immediate setup for subsequent diversification reactions.
Nevertheless, iodobromide 2n exhibited superior
S _ { \mathrm { N } } 2 ^ { \prime }
reactivity with p-thiocresol (4g, 80% yield 1:5.7 E/Z) followed
by copper-catalyzed amide coupling of the vinyl iodide to
aford enamide 4h in 59% isolated yield.<sup>21,22</sup>
As anticipated, vicinal vinylic, allylic dibromides proved to
be the best compromise between the bromochlorides and the
iodohalides, owing to the lability of the allylic bromide
combined with the better stability of the vinyl bromide.
Probenecid-derived dibromide 2y could undergo highly
selective regiodivergent substitutions to aford vinyl bromides
4i and 4j in synthetically useful yields. Notably, palladium-
catalyzed Tsuji-Trost substitution with benzenesulfinate was
feasible without significant β-halo elimination to the allene, as
observed with other dihalide variants.<sup>23</sup>
In conclusion, we have developed a catalytic dihalogenation
of monosubstituted allenes, leading to vicinal vinylic and allylic
dihalides. Products were isolated in up to 93% yield and >20:1
regioselectivity using common electrophilic reagents in
combination with thionyl halides as latent nucleophiles
activated by simple Lewis base catalysts. This convenient
strategy for the synthesis of bromochlorides, iodochlorides,
iodobromides, and dibromides employs noncryogenic reaction
temperatures and low catalyst loadings of 1 mol %. The
resulting dihalides were evaluated as useful building blocks for
the preparation of a diverse range of functionalized di- and
trisubstituted alkenes.
